rationale: A wins because it keeps the story on rails: "Does \"hundreds of millions of queries\" add up to a real shopping channel for Perplexity?" turns the company's vanity scale into a testable retail-tech story. B has sharper elbows, but "Perplexity Moves Into Commerce, Putting AI Search Directly Against Google Shopping and Amazon" smuggles in competitors and market structure the update did not supply. A is pitchable after proof checks; B needs factual cleanup before anyone should put it near a reporter.
gaps_in_A: "subscription revenue alone hasn't proven out for AI answer engines" is outside the supplied update; either source it or cut it.
"The publishers threatening Perplexity with lawsuits are the same ones it's now offering to pay" overstates the fact pattern unless those specific publishers are eligible or invited.
"the receipts its last valuation is betting on" is a useful investor frame, but without investor comment it remains a hypothesis and A correctly flags that as a proof gap.
gaps_in_B: "Putting AI Search Directly Against Google Shopping and Amazon" imports competitors not in the update and turns a shopping launch into a head-to-head fight without evidence.
"for the first time, an AI search product is inserting itself into the transaction" is an unsupported first-ever claim. Never write first unless you can prove first.
"publisher participation appears opt-in; content is cited regardless" is not in the update; that is a legal and publisher-relations landmine, not a casual inference.
"The prevailing framing of this launch is \"Perplexity makes peace with publishers\"" invents a narrative instead of proving one.
